paragraphs: Every decision a person makes carries an outcome, but when choices are driven by greed, vanity, or discontentment, the results can be devastating. Both W.W. Jacobs' short story "The Monkey's Paw" and Guy de Maupassant's "The Necklace" explore this reality through characters who try to reach beyond their station in life. A central theme shared by both works is that attempting to alter one's circumstances through reckless choices or dishonesty leads to severe and unavoidable consequences. Whether characters are tampering with supernatural forces or hiding the truth out of pride, their actions demonstrate that escaping reality often costs far more than people expect.

In "The Monkey's Paw," Jacobs shapes this theme by drawing directly on traditional folklore and classic storytelling tropes. When Sergeant-Major Morris explains the origins of the talisman, he reveals that an Indian holy man created it as a moral lesson: "He wanted to show that fate ruled people’s lives, and that those who interfered with it did so to their sorrow." Furthermore, Mrs. White jokingly observes that the magical object "sounds like the Arabian Nights," referencing famous Eastern tales about genies, wishes, and dangerous enchantments. By framing the paw through these ancient traditions, Jacobs prepares the reader for the danger of tampering with destiny. Mr. White ignores the warnings of the experienced soldier, who explicitly tells him to "pitch it on the fire again like a sensible man." Instead, Mr. White chooses to pull the paw from the flames and make a wish, showing that human curiosity and the desire for unearned wealth can blind people to catastrophic consequences.

Similarly, "The Necklace" demonstrates how prideful choices lead to irreversible ruin. Madame Loisel is so obsessed with appearing wealthy that she borrows a diamond necklace to fit in with high society. However, when she loses the piece of jewelry, she chooses secrecy and false pride over honesty. Rather than confessing the loss to her wealthy friend, she decides to secretly replace it, plunging herself and her husband into crushing poverty. As the narrator notes, "That dreadful debt must be paid. She would pay it." For ten miserable years, she faces "the horrible existence of the needy" and works until she becomes "strong and hard and rough." The narrator reflects on the fragility of her choices, asking, "How small a thing is needed to make or ruin us!" The final irony is delivered when Madame Forestier reveals that the original jewelry was only cheap imitation: "Oh, my poor Mathilde! Why, my necklace was paste! It was worth at most only five hundred francs!" Madame Loisel’s foolish choice to preserve her vanity instead of simply telling the truth costs her an entire decade of her youth and happiness.

Ultimately, both stories serve as timeless warnings about the gravity of human decisions. In "The Monkey's Paw," Mr. White pays for his curiosity and interference with fate, while in "The Necklace," Mathilde Loisel destroys her future through superficial pride and deceit. This theme remains deeply relevant today, where modern culture frequently pushes people to chase superficial status, instant gratification, or quick fixes. Whether someone is hiding a mistake to avoid embarrassment or making impulsive decisions to obtain things they have not earned, the lessons of Jacobs and Maupassant still apply. Real life cannot be repaired with magic wishes or masked by deception, and every choice will eventually demand payment in full.

In 'The Monkey's Paw,' Jacobs uses older traditions to shape the theme that interfering with fate leads to terrible results. Sergeant-Major Morris explains that 'It had a spell put on it by an old fakir, a very holy man. He wanted to show that fate ruled people’s lives, and that those who interfered with it did so to their sorrow.' The old fakir put a spell on the dried paw because he want to show that destiny should not be tested. When Mrs. White hears about the wishes, she laughs and says it 'Sounds like the Arabian Nights,' which shows how she treats ancient magic like a harmless myth. Morris threw the talisman straight into the hearth, Mr. White quickly pulled it out before it burned. Because Herbert and his mother thought the magical artifact was merely a joke from an old tale. By ignoring Morris's serious warning that 'If you keep it, don’t blame me for what happens,' Mr. White chooses to tempt fate and suffers the ultimate loss.

Similarly, 'The Necklace' proves that hiding the truth and pursuing vanity will lead to endless suffering. Mathilde Loisel borrows a gorgeous piece of jewelry to look high class at a ball, but when she loses it, she conceals the mistake. She chose to lie instead of telling the truth that decision cost her ten years of terrible labor. Madame Loisel and her husband works for ten long years to repay the huge loans, and 'She came to know what heavy housework meant and the odious cares of the kitchen.' After she sacrifices her beauty and strength, she discovers from Madame Forestier that the original necklace was fake: 'Why, my necklace was paste! It was worth at most only five hundred francs!' Mathilde chose pride over honesty, and that single choice completely ruined her life.

In conclusion, both stories teach the valuable lesson that our choices have irreversible outcomes. In the modern world, this theme is still very relevant because people often rush after luxury or take dangerous shortcuts to get what they desire. For example, people today go into deep financial debt just to show off designer items on social media, or they ignore wise advice from others like Mr. White did with the paw. If people do not think carefully about the consequences before making big decisions, they might end up paying a heavy price just like Madame Loisel and the White family.

In both "The Monkey's Paw" by W.W. Jacobs and "The Necklace" by Guy de Maupassant, the authors demonstrate that human choices bring serious consequences that can alter a person's entire life. When people are dissatisfied with what they have, they often make reckless decisions to obtain wealth or status. Both stories convey the theme that trying to force fate or pretending to be someone you are not leads directly to suffering and regret. Through the experiences of their characters, both authors show that every single decision carries a lasting cost.

In "The Monkey's Paw," Mr. White makes the terrible choice to rescue the talisman and wish on it even though he is repeatedly warned. Jacobs draws on older storytelling traditions like the Arabian Nights and Eastern tales of magic to build this theme about destiny. The sergeant-major explains that an old fakir put a spell on the dried paw because "he wanted to show that fate ruled people's lives, and that those who interfered with it did so to their sorrow." The soldier calls the maker a fakir, which means a fake person who tricks people with cheap illusions. When Herbert doubts the paw, the soldier treats him like a "presumptuous youth," meaning Herbert was acting like an extremely polite boy who knows how to be quiet. Furthermore, Mrs. White jokes that the paw "sounds like the Arabian Nights," which reminds the reader of ancient tales where genies grant wishes that always come with hidden traps. Mr. White wanted money so he took the paw from the fire and then he kept it because he wanted wishes and his friend told him not to. His choice to meddle with fate directly results in the tragic death of his only son.

Similarly, "The Necklace" shows how an arrogant choice can ruin someone for years. After Madame Loisel loses Madame Forestier's borrowed jewelry, she chooses to secretly buy a replacement instead of confessing her mistake. This dishonest decision forces her family into a decade of poverty to repay their loans. The story describes her harsh labor: "She washed the soiled linen, the shirts and the dishcloths, which she dried upon a line." This quote shows that she washed dirty laundry and hung it outside to dry, which proves that people always suffer when they make bad choices. To pay for the replacement, the Loisels survived the "rates of usury," which means the money lenders were being very useful and generous to them. At the end, Madame Forestier reveals that her original necklace was actually made of "paste," meaning it was crafted out of sticky white glue and paper instead of diamonds. If Mathilde had simply told the truth immediately, ten years of misery would have been avoided.

In conclusion, "The Monkey's Paw" and "The Necklace" both prove that our choices shape our future and that shortcuts often backfire. In Jacobs's tale, a man chooses to tamper with destiny, while in Maupassant's story, a woman chooses pride over honesty. This lesson is especially relevant to life today. In our modern world, people constantly make questionable choices on social media to appear wealthy or chase fast money, only to find themselves trapped in debt or losing what matters most. Just like Mr. White and Madame Loisel, we have to recognize the true weight of our decisions before the consequences catch up to us.

Despite hearing that the previous owner's final wish was for death, Mr. White chooses to rescue the paw from the hearth after Morris urges him to '[p]itch it on the fire again like a sensible man.' By choosing curiosity and the desire for unearned fortune over wise counsel, Mr. White actively interferes with fate, ensuring that his family will suffer the sorrow promised by the fakir.

In a similar manner, Guy de Maupassant explores the destructive power of human choices in 'The Necklace,' though through a realistic lens rather than a supernatural one. Madame Loisel's downfall does not happen simply because she loses Madame Forestier's jewelry, but because she chooses pride and deceit over honesty. Instead of confessing the loss to her friend, she and her husband borrow an enormous sum of money to secretly replace it, locking themselves into a decade of crushing debt. As a result of this decision, '[s]he washed the dishes, using her dainty fingers and rosy nails on greasy pots and pans' and transformed into a worn-out, impoverished woman. The brutal irony of her choice is revealed when Madame Forestier tells her, 'Oh, my poor Mathilde! Why, my necklace was paste! It was worth at most only five hundred francs!' Mathilde’s choice to protect her social image rather than tell the truth robbed her of ten years of her life for a piece of cheap costume jewelry.

Ultimately, both stories deliver an enduring warning about personal responsibility that remains relevant to modern life. Today, people are constantly tempted by get-rich-quick schemes, shortcuts, and the urge to project a flawless image on social media to impress others. Just like Mr. White meddling with ancient magic or Madame Loisel ruining her future over a fake diamond necklace, modern individuals often choose vanity and instant gratification without considering the long-term price. Morris explains that an old fakir put a spell on the paw because "He wanted to show that fate ruled people’s lives, and that those who interfered with it did so to their sorrow." Jacobs draws directly on older eastern traditions and folklore here, specifically using the fakir and the magical wish motif to structure his lesson about morality. Later, Mrs. White even jokes that it "Sounds like the Arabian Nights," showing how the family treats ancient mystical warnings like an entertaining fairy tale rather than a real danger. Despite Morris throwing the paw into the fire and telling Mr. White to "Pitch it on the fire again like a sensible man," Mr. White rescues it and makes a wish anyway. His choice to interfere with fate directly causes the death of his son Herbert, fulfilling the fakir's warning that selfish wishes come with unbearable prices.

Similarly, Guy de Maupassant explores how poor choices lead to suffering in "The Necklace," though his characters are undone by human pride rather than supernatural magic. After Mathilde Loisel loses Madame Forestier's borrowed necklace, she and her husband make the terrible decision to hide the truth and secretly purchase a replacement. The narrator explains that Mathilde accepted her ruin with sudden pride, thinking, "That dreadful debt must be paid. She would pay it." Mathilde clearly deserved to suffer ten years of hard labor because people who borrow jewelry never care about honesty anyway. For an entire decade, the couple sacrifices their home, youth, and happiness to pay off massive debts, only to discover at the end that the original necklace was a fake when Madame Forestier cries, "Oh, my poor Mathilde! Why, my necklace was paste! It was worth at most only five hundred francs!" If Mathilde had chosen honesty over vanity, her family would have avoided utter ruin, which proves how prideful choices lead to severe consequences.

Ultimately, both stories highlight how human nature often blinds people to the true risks of their choices until it is far too late to fix them. Even though "The Monkey's Paw" uses a magical talisman and "The Necklace" relies on realistic fiction, both show that trying to project a false lifestyle or force fate to grant unearned rewards brings disaster. This theme remains deeply relevant today, especially in a world driven by social media and instant gratification. Many people make reckless financial decisions or hide mistakes just to appear wealthy and impress their peers, ignoring the long-term impact on their future. As both Jacobs and Maupassant illustrate, our everyday choices determine our lives, and trying to cheat reality usually costs far more than anyone expects.
